title: Nonstandard usage
jupyter: python3

Although Starsim is primarily intended as an agent-based disease model, due to its modular structure, it can be used for other applications as well. This guide describes how Starsim can be used (1) as a compartmental disease model, and (2) as a general-purpose agent-based model.


## Compartmental modeling

Much of Starsim's power comes from how it handles agents. However, agent-based modeling may be too slow or too complex for some problems. In Starsim 4, a disease declared from states and transitions can be run as a compartmental model as well as agents: as a deterministic ODE (`solver='ode'`), or as a stochastic compartmental model (`solver='binomial'` or `solver='gillespie'`). Under `solver='auto'` (the default), a model in which every part has a compartmental form runs as an ODE.

### Setting up the model

Here we will define a simple susceptible-infectious-recovered-susceptible (SIRS) model, in which immunity wanes. Note that the model runs extremely fast, since a three-state compartmental model runs about as fast as an agent-based model with three agents!

```{python}
import starsim as ss
ss.options(jupyter=True)
import sciris as sc
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

S, I, R = ss.states(3)
infection = S >> I @ ss.peryear(0.8) * I # Starsim's time units work as for agents
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.peryear(0.1)
waning    = R >> S @ ss.peryear(0.05)
sirs = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, waning, init_prev=0.01)

# Run the compartmental simulation (csim)
csim = ss.Sim(sirs, stop=100, dt=ss.years(0.1))
csim.run()
csim.plot()
```

The sim prints the solver it chose, and why. `csim.solvers()` shows which solvers can run the model.

Let's compare to the same model run as agents. Nothing in the model changes: only the solver, and the number of agents:

```{python}
abm = ss.Sim(sirs, stop=100, dt=ss.years(0.1), solver='abm', n_agents=10_000, verbose=0)
abm.run()

# Plot the results
plt.figure()
for sim, label in [(csim, 'ODE'), (abm, 'Agents')]:
    plt.plot(sim.timevec, sim.results.sirs.n_I, label=label)
plt.xlabel('Time (years)')
plt.ylabel('Number infectious')
plt.legend()
sc.boxoff()
plt.show()
```

The results are very similar, apart from the noise in the agent-based run, which is a stochastic process. Note that the compartmental version runs more than 10 times faster than the agent-based version. Does this mean that compartmental models are better than agent-based models? If all you want to simulate is a simple SIRS model, then ... the answer is probably yes! Adding a contact network (e.g. `networks='random'`), or anything else that exists only per agent, makes the same model run as agents.

Agents and the chain-binomial solver (`solver='binomial'`) take whole steps, so they differ from the ODE by an amount that grows with the step. For an SIR with R0 3 and 10 days infectious, a daily step puts the peak 2 to 4% higher and 2 to 3 days later than the exact answer, while a weekly step puts it 12 to 32% higher and 10 to 24 days later. For a seasonal SIRS at a daily step, `binomial` has about 19% more people infectious on average (up to 53% at times). A smaller `dt`, or `substeps=` for `binomial`, brings these down; `solver='gillespie'` does not take whole steps. The sim notes when a transition is fast compared with the step, and `sim.check_dt()` shows how much a smaller step changes your model's results.

A compartmental model can also still be written as code, as a module whose `step()` updates counts that it holds as plain numbers. This works, but it runs only as written, and it does not get `describe()`, `equations()`, or the other solvers.

## Epiverse Epidemics: School closure model

This example adapts the example from the _Epidemics_ v0.4.0 R package:

[https://epiverse-trace.github.io/epidemics/](https://epiverse-trace.github.io/epidemics/)

Note that it does not use the same level of detail as the original in terms of the population or contact matrices, but produces similar results. School closure is approximated by halving the susceptibility and transmissibility of children while schools are closed, with `ss.modify()`. A modifier never overwrites the quantity it changes, so nothing has to be restored when schools reopen. Infections by age are results of the disease once the sim is stratified by age.

```{python}
import pandas as pd
import starsim as ss

sir = ss.SIR(
    init_prev = 0.001,
    beta = ss.perday(1/100),
    dur_inf = ss.days(20.0),
)

# Intervention: close schools from day 50 to day 80
children = ss.People.age < 20
closure = dict(multiply=0.5, where=children, start=ss.days(50), stop=ss.days(80))
close_schools = [
    ss.modify(sir.rel_sus, **closure),
    ss.modify(sir.rel_trans, **closure),
]

# Run the model
sim = ss.Sim(
    people = ss.People(n_agents=20e3, age_data=pd.read_csv('test_data/nigeria_age.csv')),
    diseases = sir,
    networks = 'random',
    interventions = close_schools,
    stratify = dict(age=[0, 20, 40]), # Results by age
    start = ss.days(0),
    stop = ss.days(300),
    verbose = False,
)
sim.run()

# Plot infections by age
sim.results.sir.n_I.by('age').plot()
for day in [50, 80]:
    plt.axvline(day, linestyle=':')
plt.show()
```

While the Starsim version is longer than the Epidemics version, note that Epidemics has built-in contacts interventions. Starsim's modifiers and stratified results do the same jobs in a few lines, and a custom intervention or analyzer written as code is always available for anything they cannot say.

## Mesa: Wealth model

This example illustrates a simple "wealth model", in which each agent starts with a single unit of wealth, and on each timestep, every agent with more than zero wealth gives one unit of wealth to another agent.

This tutorial is adapted from the following example:

[https://mesa.readthedocs.io/en/stable/tutorials/intro_tutorial.html](https://mesa.readthedocs.io/en/stable/tutorials/intro_tutorial.html)

### Setting up the model

We could define the wealth model as any type of module, since they all can store states and update them. Here we will define it as a plain `ss.Module` (though it could equally well be a subclass of `ss.Intervention` or `ss.Demographics`, if you are so inclined), passed to the sim as a demographics module. All we need to do is update the `wealth` state (which we can store inside the "intervention"), and we can also use this class to track the wealth distribution over time and plot it. The full model looks like this:

```{python}
"""
Define the classic agent-based "wealth model" in Starsim
"""

# Imports
import numpy as np
import starsim as ss
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Define the model
class WealthModel(ss.Module):
    """ A simple wealth transfer model"""
    
    def init_post(self, bins=10):
        """ Define custom model attributes """
        super().init_post()
        self.npts = len(self.sim) # Number of timepoints
        self.n_agents = len(self.sim.people) # Number of agents
        self.wealth = np.ones(self.n_agents) # Initial wealth of each agent
        self.bins = np.arange(bins+1) # Bins used for plotting
        self.wealth_dist = np.zeros((self.npts, len(self.bins)-1)) # Wealth distribution over time
        return
        
    def step(self):
        """ Transfer wealth between agents -- core model logic """
        givers = self.wealth > 0 # People need wealth to be givers
        receivers = np.random.choice(self.sim.people.uid, size=givers.sum()) # Anyone can be a receiver
        self.wealth[givers] -= 1 # Givers are unique, so can use vectorized version
        for receive in receivers: # Vectorized version is: np.add.at(sim.people.wealth.raw, receivers, 1)
            self.wealth[receive] += 1
        return
    
    def update_results(self):
        """ Store the wealth histogram at this time point (at the start, and after each step) """
        super().update_results()
        self.wealth_dist[self.ti,:], _ = np.histogram(self.wealth, bins=self.bins)
        return
    
    def plot(self):
        """ Plot a 2D histogram of the final wealth distribution """
        plt.figure()
        plt.bar(self.bins[:-1], self.wealth_dist[-1,:])
        plt.title('Wealth distribution at final time point')
        plt.xlabel('Wealth')
        plt.ylabel('Number of agents')
        plt.show()
        return
    
    def plot3d(self):
        """ Plot a 3D heatmap of the wealth distribution over time """
        plt.figure()
        plt.pcolor(self.wealth_dist.T, cmap='turbo')
        plt.title('Wealth distribution over time')
        plt.xlabel('Time')
        plt.ylabel('Wealth')
        plt.colorbar().set_label('Number of agents', rotation=270)
        plt.show()
        return

# Create sim inputs, including the wealth model
wealth = WealthModel()
pars = dict(
    n_agents = 100, # Number of agents
    start = 0,
    stop = 100,
    demographics = wealth,
)

# Run the model
sim = ss.Sim(pars, copy_inputs=False) # copy_inputs=False lets us reuse the "wealth" object from above
sim.run()

# Plot the results
wealth.plot()
wealth.plot3d()
```

### Comparison with Mesa

While the implementation in Starsim is similar to Mesa, there are a couple key differences:

- Because Starsim's people object is vectorized, the wealth definition and update is vectorized as well.
- Both Mesa and Starsim versions of the model are quite simple, but there is a little less boilerplate in the Starsim version.
